title: Pointers and dynamic arrays
overview: Module 15 introduces pointers. A pointer is a variable that holds another variable's memory address. It lets you read or change that variable from anywhere, and it is how C builds arrays whose size is decided while the program runs (`malloc`, `calloc`, `realloc`, `free`). The practice files are small Codeforces problems where you try out these tools.

concepts.explain: `&a` gives the address of `a`. If `int *p = &a;`, then `*p` is the value stored at that address, so reading or changing `*p` reads or changes `a`.
concepts.snippet: int a = 5; int *p = &a; *p = 10; // a is now 10

concepts.explain: Use `%p` for addresses. The exact numbers change from machine to machine and run to run. Only how they relate to each other matters.

concepts.term: Array name = address of first element
concepts.explain: `int *p = arr;` is the same as `p = &arr[0]`. `arr[i]` is shorthand for `*(arr + i)`.
`p + 1` moves ahead by one element, not by one byte. For `int*` that is usually 4 bytes, and for `char*` it is 1 byte.
`int **y = &x;` holds the address of a pointer. `*y` is `x`, which is an address, and `**y` is the int that `x` points to.

`malloc(n * sizeof(int))` sets aside memory while the program runs and doesn't clear it. `calloc(n, sizeof(int))` also sets every byte to zero. `realloc(p, newSize)` grows or shrinks the block. `free(p)` gives the memory back.
With the addresses of two variables, a temp variable and two `*` assignments swap their values.

files.title: Pointer basics: &, * and changing through a pointer
files.what: Makes a pointer `b` to `a`, prints the addresses, reads `a` through `*b`, then changes `a` by assigning to `*b`.
steps: `int a = 5; int *b = &a;` makes `b` hold the address of `a`.
`&a` and `b` print the same address. `&b` is a different address: the place where the pointer itself is stored.
files.output_note: `Address of a` and `Value of b` show the same hex address. `Address of b` is different. Then come the values 5, 5, 10 and 10. Your addresses will be different from the ones shown here.
files.watch_out: `val` is a copy, not a link. If you changed `*b` after the last `val = *b`, `val` would keep the old value.

check.q: What is the difference between `b` and `&b`?
check.a: `b` is the address it stores (the address of `a`). `&b` is the address of the pointer variable itself.

files.title: Arrays as pointers and pointer arithmetic
files.what: Shows that an array name holds the address of its first element, and that `p + 1` moves ahead by the size of the pointed type.
steps: `int *p = arr;`: printing `arr` and `p` gives the same address.
`p + 1` is the address of `arr[1]`, which is 4 bytes further on.
For `int *x`, `x` and `x + 1` are also 4 bytes apart.
For `char *y`, `y` and `y + 1` are only 1 byte apart.
files.output_note: Look at the last hex digits. The first address and `p` match. The next element is `+4` (…30 → …34), `x` and `x+1` are 4 apart (…2C → …30), and `y` and `y+1` are 1 apart (…2B → …2C).
files.watch_out: `p + 1` never means "one byte further". The step is always `sizeof(*p)`.

check.q: If `p` points at address 1000 and is a `double*` (8 bytes), where does `p + 2` point?

files.title: Pointer to pointer
files.what: Builds the chain `y → x → a` and shows what each level of `*` gives you.
steps: `int **y = &x;` points to `x`, so `y` and `&x` print the same address.
`*y` is the value stored in `x`, which is `&a`.
`**y` follows both steps and reaches `a`, which is 5. That is the same as `*x`.
files.output_note: Each line shows two equal things: `y` and `&x`, `*y` and `&a`, `**y` and `a` (5 and 5), `**y` and `*x` (5 and 5).

files.title: Swap two variables via pointers
files.what: Swaps `a` and `b` using only the pointers `x` and `y` and a temp variable.
files.output_note: `Before swapping: a = 5, b = 8`, then `After swapping: a = 8, b = 5`.
files.watch_out: The comment "dereferencing temp" is wrong. `temp` is a plain int, not a pointer.

check.a: Without it, `*x = *y` would overwrite `a`'s old value before it could be copied into `b`.

files.title: malloc, realloc and free
files.what: Sets aside room for 5 ints, fills them, grows the block to 10 with `realloc`, fills the new part, prints everything, and frees the memory.
steps: `malloc(5 * sizeof(int))` returns a block for 5 ints. `arr[i] = i + 1` fills it with 1 to 5.
The old pointer is saved in `temp` in case `realloc` fails.
`realloc(arr, 10 * sizeof(int))` makes the block bigger. The first 5 values are kept.
If the result is `NULL`, the program puts the old pointer back. Otherwise it fills indexes 5 to 9 with 6 to 10 and prints all 10.
files.watch_out: `malloc` memory isn't cleared, so read only what you have written. Use `calloc` if you need zeros. After `free`, don't use `arr` again.

check.q: What does `realloc` do with the old values when it has to move the block?
check.a: It copies them into the new block and frees the old one.

files.title: Add
files.what: Reads two numbers and prints their sum.
files.watch_out: The practice sheet asks you to do this with pointers or a function. This version adds directly. Try `int *p = &x, *q = &y; printf("%d", *p + *q);`.

check.q: How would you write it with a function?
check.a: `int add(int a, int b){ return a + b; }`, then `printf("%d", add(x, y));`.

files.title: Swap
files.what: Reads `X` and `Y` and prints them swapped. It is the same pointer swap as `swap.c`, applied to input.

check.a: Yes, and the judge would accept it. The point of the exercise is to practise the pointer swap.

files.title: Min & Max of three numbers
files.what: Starts with `A` as both the min and the max, then updates them using `B` and `C`.
steps: If `B` is smaller than `min`, update `min`. If `B` is bigger than `max`, update `max`.

check.q: Why start `min` at `A` instead of at 0?
check.a: 0 might be smaller than every input, for example if all of them are positive. That would give the wrong min.

files.title: Summation (absolute)
files.what: Should print the absolute value of the total, but this code adds up the absolute value of each number instead.
steps: For each number, add `abs(num)` to the `long long` `sum`.
files.watch_out: **Wrong formula:** the judge wants the absolute value of the sum, not the sum of absolute values. Add the raw numbers, then print `llabs(sum)`. Also, `abs` works on `int`, so use `llabs` for `long long`.

check.q: For `-1 2 -3`, what are |sum| and the sum of |values|?

files.title: Replacement
files.what: Changes every positive number to 1 and every negative number to 2. Zeros stay as they are.
steps: If `A[i] > 0`, set it to 1. Otherwise, if `A[i] < 0`, set it to 2. A zero matches neither test and is left alone.
Print the array, with each value followed by a space.
files.watch_out: The practice sheet suggests a dynamic array and walking it with a pointer: `int *A = malloc(N * sizeof(int));` and `*(A + i)`.

check.q: Why must the negative check be `else if` rather than a separate `if` placed after the first one?
check.a: Here both forms happen to work, because a 1 is never negative. `else if` makes it clear that the cases can't both apply.

recap: `&` gives an address. `*` follows an address to the value stored there.
An array name is the address of its first element, and `arr[i]` means `*(arr + i)`.
`p + 1` moves ahead by one element (`sizeof` the type).
`malloc` and `calloc` set memory aside, `realloc` resizes it, and `free` gives it back.
To swap through pointers, use `temp = *x; *x = *y; *y = temp;`.

check_yourself.a: 11. `p` points at `x`, so it sees the change.

check_yourself.q: `int a[4] = {1,2,3,4}; int *p = a + 2; p++; *p = 100;` What is the array now?
What is the difference between `malloc(5*sizeof(int))` and `calloc(5, sizeof(int))`?
check_yourself.a: Both set aside room for 5 ints. `calloc` also fills it with zeros.

body: Every house on a street has a number. When you want a parcel delivered you do not carry the house to the shop; you give the number, and the parcel reaches the right door. The number is not the house, but it is enough to find the house.

A computer's memory is one very long street. Every byte of it has a number, its **address**, and every variable you have declared so far has been sitting at one of those numbered places. This module is about holding the address instead of the value.

`int a = 5;` does two things that you can now look at separately. It sets aside four bytes somewhere in memory, and it writes 5 into them. The compiler remembers where those bytes are; until now you never had to.

`&a` is that address, and you have been typing it for months inside `scanf("%d", &a)` without thinking about it: `scanf` has to put the number somewhere, so you give it the address. Printed with `%p`, one run looked like this:
The exact number differs on every machine and every run, so do not try to remember it. Only how addresses relate to each other matters.

A pointer is simply a variable whose value is an address. `int *b = &a;` creates `b` and puts the address of `a` inside it. It is a house number written on a slip of paper, and the slip of paper itself lies in another house:

The star means "go there". `*b` reads the 5 back. And `*b = 10;` writes 10 into `a`'s own bytes, so `a` becomes 10 even though the name `a` never appears in that line. **That is what is new**: until now, the only way to change `a` was to write `a`.
intro.trace:
variable   value          address
   a       5              0x...17f8
   b       0x...17f8      0x...1800

 b   the address of a
&b   where b itself is kept
*b   5: go to that address and read

body: **A second example.** An array name is already an address. For `int arr[5]`, plain `arr` is the address of `arr[0]`, so `int *p = arr;` and `int *p = &arr[0];` are the same line, and `arr[i]` is shorthand for `*(arr + i)`. Adding 1 to a pointer moves it on by one whole element, not by one byte: for an `int*` the address goes up by 4, for a `char*` by 1.

**A third example.** Swapping two variables needs no new idea. With `int *x = &a, *y = &b;`, the three lines `temp = *x; *x = *y; *y = temp;` exchange the values of `a` and `b` through their addresses.

The second half of the module uses addresses for something you could not do before. Until now an array's size was decided while you were writing the program. You guess a big number, `int arr[1000]`, and hope: with 5 numbers most of it is wasted, with 2000 you write past the end. And once the block exists it can never be made bigger.
`malloc` asks for a block of memory while the program runs and gives back its address, which is why the answer goes into a pointer:

`calloc(n, sizeof(int))` does the same and fills the block with zeros, while `malloc` leaves whatever rubbish was in those bytes, so read only what you have written. `realloc(arr, newSize)` resizes the block and keeps the values already in it. `free(arr)` hands the memory back, and after that you must not use the pointer again.

The programs below go one step at a time: `&` and `*` on a single variable, an array walked with a pointer, a pointer holding the address of another pointer, the swap, then `malloc`, `realloc` and `free`. After those come five short judge problems.
